utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to my learned friends of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Later this morning, also, Ms. Patty Sellers will join the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones. I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, before we bring in the new witness, what are your intentions? Who is leading this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, my intention this morning is to do a very brief direct-examination of the individual who took the pictures of the houses that were damaged and the monuments that were damaged in the various villages in our indictment, as well as some of the other village that were made reference to by numerous witnesses. During that examination, I have selected a series of photographs, not many, I would think less than 20, for him to sort of describe to -- to Your Honours how, in his opinion, the damage to the houses occurred. And I think it will assist the Trial Chamber, as you review the photographs later on, and as you make your own assessment as to how the damage occurred. I should add, Your Honour, excuse me, that this individual has a wealth of experience as a crime scene technician, almost 25 years, and I believe that his opinion with respect to the damage to the buildings that he observed himself two years after the incidents will -- I think, will be very illuminating to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm somewhat dismayed that he's going to be giving that sort of evidence, because the exercise will be greatly protracted, I'm afraid, because it wouldn't do simply for my learned friend to take a few photographs and to ask this person his opinion about how the damage was caused for the following reason: This person took photographs in July 1994, and possibly later, so we're talking about up to maybe two years, nearly, after these events occurred. In our submission, firstly, he doesn't know when -- it's impossible for him to say anything of when any damage was caused. But also, as to how it was caused, we would have submissions and cross-examination on that subject. And so if my learned friend proposed to elicit that evidence from him, then we will have to show him photographs and say, Well, surely this was caused by a shell, surely this is consistent with people taking away roof tiles, surely in this case -- Your Honour gets the idea of what the exercise will be like. We certainly wouldn't finish today. I'm happy to do that, and I've prepared on the basis that that's cross-examination which I'd have to conduct. But certainly it would at least take an hour and a half or two hours, on our part, to go through the many photographs where we say there's either no damage evident, or damage which is consistent with, as we say, with some innocent explanation. We anticipated, based on the statement of this witness, which we only received, after all, in August of this year, and it was served after most of the statements, but -- fair enough, but that statement was simply, I took these photographs on this date. And we're perfectly happy with him giving that evidence, and I could cross-examine him very briefly on that basis. But if he's going to come forward as some sort of expert to say, in my view, this was arson, or in my view, this could only have been caused by human agency, then we're in for a long exercise. And that's -- that's fine. I mean, we're happy to do that, but it does affect the timing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The statements, in fact, were turned over to the Defence in August, and I believe that's when they were taken. With respect to the necessity of going into how the damage occurred, I think it's highly relevant and probative to these proceedings. I have seen the Defence cross-examine numerous witnesses and suggested to them that the houses or the buildings were, in fact, not that much by fire but maybe, possibly, by bombs and other type of heavy artillery. And I think that it would be very helpful to the Trial Chamber to clarify, in fact, how this damage occurred. Now, the fact that I have selected a few photographs is just in the interests of time. There are numerous photographs, I think there are about 90 in all. I didn't think it necessary to go through all of them, but to provide a sample for Your Honours and for this witness to explain the damage, and from his own experience, what he believes the damage could have been caused by. And I understand that the Defence would seek to examine him further on other photographs that they might think relevant, and I don't see the problem of them doing that. But in the interests of time, I simply selected a sample of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one final matter. I'm not clear now if this witness is actually being proposed as an expert, and if he is an expert, then we're going to need to know his qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the whole thing. Of course, I'm going to refrain and suggest to my two colleagues to refrain from taking a decision on whether he should be allowed to testify on what would have caused the damage to the property, and we will reserve our judgement until the time we have heard what his expertise in this area of forensic science is. From my own experience in my jurisdiction, we're talking of highly sophisticated -- or matters that require highly sophisticated expertise, particularly when you come to fire. There are few real experts on arson and on fire, and also on explosives, particularly ones we've heard that fire and explosives could be caused by Zoljas, et cetera, et cetera, so on and so forth. But anyway, when we come to that moment, we will put the question as to his expertise, then we will withdraw, retire, for a couple of minutes and decide whether to allow further questions on his --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the -- for the -- on the part of the Prosecution, we have not proposed that this witness be tendered -- submitted to the Court as an expert in fires. In fact, it's our belief that his 25 years' experience includes crime scene investigation, not only of fires but of other types of criminal investigations. So with that, I would only ask that Your Honours take that into consideration. And we're seeking to elicit tender his opinion based on his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the last 25 years, how many wars have there been in the areas where he gained all this experience, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, understood. I -- Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there's only been one war, and that's 10 years ago, 12 years ago -- MS. RICHARDSON: Your honour, I'm not suggesting that he is an expert in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honour, I'm not suggesting that he's an expert in investigating war, war crimes, or damages -- or damage to buildings as a result of war. I'm simply proposing to the Court that the Trial Chamber listen to his testimony, taking into consideration the fact that he has 25 years' experience as a crime scene -- crime scene technician, Your Honour, and that includes fires. And I would only suggest that his opinion be taken as that based on his -- based on his experience. And I say -- and I would also suggest that it's taken into consideration along with the others' opinion -- other opinion given by witnesses who were either present at the time that this occurred or later visited the site. And it was elicited from them during cross-examination how or what, in their opinion, caused damage to the buildings. And I would simply think that his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you see --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- that his testimony would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come that later on. Mr. Jones let's not -- Mr. Jones let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, it's just -- Your Honour it's just one very important point, though, which is that the question of notice and Rule 94 bis. I mean, certainly, if anyone were to come forward as an expert now, without going under the procedure under 94 bis where we would have time to consider the expert, his qualifications, that can't simply be bypassed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then just to say that a crime technician's expertise in this case is in taking photographs, that's what, in the region, these people do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way I know it, at least, is as follows: If you have a fire, you will have an expert on fire that will go on site and examine the terrain, examine the terrain, and after examining the terrain and while he is examining the terrain, he would indicate to the officer who was taking the photographs what photographs to take, but all photographs will be taken under the direction of the officer who is investigating. If it's an explosion, again -- I mean, if it's a fire, you try to identify the source of the fire; if it's an explosion, you examine all sorts of things with a view to establishing whether the explosion -- where the explosion occurred, whether it's on the inside or on the outside, and what kind of an explosive material was used, so on and so forth. I mean, this is expert -- an expert's work. As Mr. Jones has suggested, I mean, if your client -- if your witness is being put forward as an expert, then you haven't followed the procedure laid down by our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would again reiterate that he's not being put forward as an expert; he's simply being put forward as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's even more dangerous, my dear. If you are going to present this person not as an expert, but you're going to put questions to him with a view of eliciting from him his own personal opinion of what could have caused the fire or what could have caused the explosion or what could have caused the damage, knowing that he is not an expert but he has got experience, and not presenting him as an expert, that's the high -- that's highly irregular. I don't know, I will need to discuss it with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, obviously, because it's not a decision that I can take on my own. But I consider it to be highly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand the Trial Chamber's position with respect to an expert, and to have one qualified and deemed an expert before the Trial Chamber based on his experience. I am simply seeking to elicit from this witness, as we have with other witnesses, his opinion as to how this fire was caused. And we have seen that throughout this trial, Your Honour, through cross-examination, and even on direct, a series of questions put to witnesses as to how, in their opinion, the fire was caused, based on their observation, on knowledge of weaponry, et cetera. And that is all I'm seeking to elicit from this witness, Your Honour. And he is not, in our opinion, an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- on fires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- let's suspend the hearing for five minutes, until we discuss a little bit outside, and we will reconvene very soon. --- Break taken at 9.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position is as follows, and this is -- there is unanimity amongst us on this: There should not be any questions put to the witness as to what could have caused the damage or the fire or the destruction, except insofar as he may be in an obvious position to say, in other words, not as an -- not as an expert but as something that he could have observed there and then on site. But not more than that. Otherwise, there shouldn't be any questions which could present his testimony as expert testimony or testimony which goes beyond his function as a photographer. So let's bring the witness in. In any case, we will direct the questions and we will stop you if we see that you are asking questions that you shouldn't be -- that he shouldn't answer, anyway; not that you shouldn't ask, that he shouldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you need to understand that there is something very delicate here, that these photos were taken two years after -- roughly two years after the events, and we need to be extremely, extremely careful. Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that you are receiving a translation of what I am saying in English into your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is the sound level in your headphones at the right level, or would you like it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's perfect. Very soon, you will start giving evidence as a witness brought forward by the Prosecution in this case instituted against Naser Oric. Our regulations require that, before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, in the sense that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper which Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. Please read it out carefully and loudly, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that you have court experience, so I need not lose much time in trying to explain to you what the procedure is here. It's very much similar to what it is in local jurisdictions. You have been summoned here by the Office of the Prosecutor, as their own witness, but now that you are testifying, you are the Tribunal's witness. And consequence number one is that, because of this, but also and primarily because of your solemn declaration, your responsibility, your obligation towards this Tribunal is to answer all questions that are put to you truthfully and fully, to the best of your ability, irrespective of who is putting the questions to you, irrespective of whether the questions are being put by the Prosecution or by the Defence. You cannot discriminate between one and the other, or favour one or the other. The Prosecution will go first. You will be asked a series of questions, and then -- by Ms. Richardson, and she will then be followed by Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel for Naser Oric in this case. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please confirm the following information: You were born on the 24th of January, 1955, and you reside in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you joined the police department in 1975, and in 1981, you were transferred to the Directorate of the Criminal Investigations Police in Belgrade, and that is the forensic team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1975. A small correction, though, service in 1981 that I was transferred to the forensic team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you qualified as a crime scene technician during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are presently the chief of the photo laboratory of the Department of Forensics, and that is with the Directorate of the Criminal Investigations Police in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the labs within our administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been the chief of the photo laboratory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Sixth year running.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that period of time - when I say "the period of time," from 1981 to presently - you have investigated a variety of crimes, and that includes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, I take objection to the use of the word "you have investigated a series of crimes." He is not an investigator, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is directed, in the course of investigations -- and please confirm what I am saying: As a forensic photographer, do you work on your own, on your own initiative, or are you given directions by the persons who are investigating a crime on a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether you may not understand the nature of my work, I will certainly make sure to set them right during my testimony, wherever misunderstandings arise. What you've just said, Your Honour, is quite correct. We are on call. We go to the crime scene. We focus on whatever material evidence can be found at the scene of crime, and forward them also to other forensic teams working on the same case. Forensic medicine is also part of this, but not my department. That is not within my personal remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the course of an investigation on a crime scene, following the report of a crime, who would conduct the investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our line of work, and under our present legislation, the investigating magistrate conducts the investigations. We are merely at his disposal. He makes a request to do whatever he deems necessary in a given case. We then do it for him, whether he wants photographs, whether he wants specific packages of material evidence, until all these are further processed, at his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will the investigating magistrate be accompanied by experts in his investigation? For example, if we're talking of a fire that has taken place in a building, and one is to establish whether that fire was accidental or whether it was arson, criminal, would there be an expert on fire assisting the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, it's quite necessary in cases like these, since, during a fire, if that is what you have in mind, changes occur from hour to hour, or rather, from minute to minute. It's usually important for an expert to arrive at the crime scene as soon as possible, even during a fire, before the fire is even out, because that makes it possible for him to get a privileged insight into what occurred. He can take samples during and after the fire which may lead him to certain conclusions on the case, specifically on what caused the fire and what the total damage might be. But this is only something that you can conclude after all these stages of the process have been followed through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you these questions. I know the answers already because I started my career as an investigating magistrate way back in 1977, so I know exactly what the procedure is, and I know that it is pretty much the same throughout the whole of Europe. My next question: If we are still talking of a fire, and the magistrate who will be the one who will do least at the time, because there will be the expert who will be assisted by an entire team of forensic experts at the time, and let's take it that you are there while the fire expert is investigating the fire, what could have possibly caused it, and so on and so forth, the photos that you will take, will these photos be taken upon the direction, as you are directed, by the expert on fire, or will you just go around and start shooting photos without any instructions or without any direction from anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You made a reference to forensic medicine in your question. The forensic medicine team only ever comes in if, during a fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I never mentioned forensic medicine. I don't know what the translation or interpretation may have been. Forensic team, forensic team, forensic scientists, I'm referring to. Forensic medicine comes in if there has been a death or someone who has been injured. But leave forensic medicine out for the time being. My question mainly elicits the following answer: In taking photos on the scene of the crime when the investigation is taking place, do you go around taking those photos you think you ought to take, or do you take photos which -- as per the directive or direction of the experts? And then my next question will be very much something related to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question both times. It's just that there may have been a misinterpretation in relation to forensic medicine being mentioned, although that team too is sometimes part of an investigation. But as concerns what you just asked me, what we tend to do is, when a fire occurs in a given building, to try to make it to the scene as soon as possible, regardless of the fact that the fire may still be raging. Why do we do this? Because that enables us to take photographs of the progress of a fire until experts on specific individual fields arrive at the scene. In our legislation, there are several different branches of experts. We have different kinds of technicians, and a team that investigates a fire covers all the different aspects of a fire. What I said about taking photographs of the initial stages of the fire, this is something that needs to be done on an independent basis, because fire changes throughout its progress. Once the ground is cleared, once the scene of arson is cleared, and you can search for causes and take samples, it is then that experts, pursuant to their own observations, request us to take photographs of certain sections, of certain objects. This is the procedure with the criminal police in Belgrade, and this is how it has been for -- over the last 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for the time being I'll stop here, I will not ask further questions. I think he's given us enough lead to be in a position to decide later on, as we go along, what questions to allow and what questions not to allow. I do have, however, one final -- one final question to the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: two years ago, and I tell you, "Now, please, Mr. Jankovic, could you photograph this building from inside and from outside" - there is no inquiring magistrate, no investigating magistrate, there is no one to give you instructions what to do - what would you do? What would you concentrate our camera or focus your camera upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This hypothetical case is very much like what I had to do in this specific case, the case that I'm appearing here for. I did the only thing that was possible for me at the time. It is a very fundamental action in forensic procedure. I took photographs of the general crime scene. Depending on when an individual fire occurred, whether it occurred today or whenever it was observed, or if maybe a building that has burned down is being observed after a great many years, one must be fully conscious of the fact that changes, quite many changes, in fact, tend to occur on these buildings, over time. This is a fundamental skill that an expert like me possesses. Traces and indicia simply disappear or rot away. It is only with great difficulty, and after a lot of work, that one may be able to reach a conclusion on how a certain building burned down. However, there are normally basic indications in these cases based on which one can give an opinion; at any rate, not a very specific opinion on the cause of a fire or the time a fire occurred, especially not after a great deal of time has already elapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Richardson, he is all yours. Thank you, Mr. Jankovic, for those explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, please confirm your educational background, briefly, for us. You received training in secondary school for criminal scene technician.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Not quite, if I may be allowed to explain. I started specialising in my job at the secondary education stage. I was specialising in traffic and transport. And then once I obtained that degree of specialisation, I was able to get a job with the crime technicians department. What you do then is you attend a course which gives you the sufficient experience to gain an insight into how crime technicians work, and also enables you to apply these specific techniques. So that would be the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've taken a number of courses and examinations that qualified you for a position as a crime scene technician.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that was initially, when I first started working in 1981. But from that moment on, I pursued further courses of specialisation and further studies, and I completed the highest school of the Ministry of the Interior, one of the subjects on that programme being a specialised subject for crime technicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also attended the University of Defence and Protection. And is this in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, as part of my continuing education. And I attend school nowadays as well, although I don't have much time. But I am continuously working on my education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of the courses you've taken at this university also included general methods of investigation, protection of fire, international law, and various other forensic-related courses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's correct. We had that in the School of Interior Affairs that I attended in Belgrade, and in addition to that, I also had a lot of subjects at the Faculty of Defence. I don't know if you want me to explain each of those relevant subjects individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. I think we have a pretty good idea of your -- of the type of courses you've taken. Now, with respect to your work experience, you mentioned to Judge Agius that you work under the direction of the magistrate judge or forensic experts. Now, with respect to fires, you have participated in the investigation of approximately 200 fires in the scope of your career.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. These were the fires occurring in the territory of the city of Belgrade, mostly fires erupting in apartments, in socially-owned facilities, also industrial facilities, theatres, and so on. I think that there was a sufficient number of cases for me not to be able to remember now each individual case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to bring your attention to 1994. Do you recall being contacted by the Commission for Gathering Information on Crimes Committed Against Humanity and International Law?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in early 1994, I was contacted by them. Mr. Ilija Simic, a judge at the District Court in Belgrade, was a judge who normally was assigned to serious criminal offences. And the criminal investigation department of the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade normally conducted the initial on-site investigation in such cases in the territory of Belgrade. Sometime in May of 1994, Mr. Zvonko Djurdumovic were contacted by this judge, and he wanted to know to what extent we would be able to assist the committee in its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you asked to do by the committee?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In the discussion we had at the time, Mr. Ilija Simic told us that the authorities of Republika Srpska had turned to them for assistance, for technical assistance, in order to evaluate, document, and photograph, as well as make sketches of damaged buildings in the territories of several municipalities in that area. The first area that we visited then was the Bratunac area. During the discussion, they gave us a list of several places that we should visit in order to see what the buildings looked like, and to make photographs. We were told that they lacked technical possibilities to do something like that, and they wanted to hear our opinion as to how that could be conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a Mr. Zvonko Djurdumovic. Could you tell us about him, and what was his field of work?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Mr. Zvonko Djurdumovic is a land surveyor, engineer specialising in land survey. He used to work at the Ministry of the Interior and then retired. When he was active, he was chief of criminal investigation department, the technical part in Belgrade. He was called by Judge Simic for a very simple reason, because he could orient himself very well on a map and knew how to survey territory. That was the reason he was invited to participate in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time that you -- let me just rephrase the question, and I have one question with respect to Mr. Djurdumovic and yourself. Did you receive official authorisation from the committee to carry out your work?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In the first discussions we had at the time, the initial discussions, we determined that we would begin with work, and our work was in its initial stage. We were given approval for going to that area in order to contact local authorities and to establish with them the methods of our work, and also who would be assisting us in our work. The official written approval for our work arrived later, but I couldn't tell you more about that, although I think that records of that should be somewhere in the court's files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to carrying out the project, what steps did you take after you received instructions from the committee? What steps did you and Mr. Djurdumovic take?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: We received from the committee a list of certain places, hamlets. I couldn't tell you exactly how many there were on the list. Mr. Djurdumovic and I worked on that list, and we approached the Bureau for Geography for the former Yugoslavia, and that bureau had records and files which traced the locations of wells and so on, and various maps. We took maps and aerial photographs from the files of that bureau. So even before we travelled to the location to conduct our work, we already had at our disposal maps and locations of various buildings and facilities that we were interested in. So with that material, we went to Bratunac municipality, and we told them that they had approached the committee for war crimes, asking for assistance, that pursuant to that, we had arrived and made plans based on the list that we had received from them. In order for us to be able to go and visit the locations, the buildings, the houses, and to take photographs and so on, and in view of the fact that this was the first time we visited that territory, we needed assistance, because we had no prior knowledge. And we also didn't have any knowledge about the locations of these objects, and no information about the owners. As a result of that, we needed assistance of local residents. So whenever we went to a certain place, local authorities would assign some local residents who had a very good knowledge of that area, and who were able to tell us who were the owners of the houses we photographed. So this is how we worked. We had these local guides who changed from one case to the next. I think we started with Jezestica. Mr. Zvonko Djurdumovic determined the position of the first house on a map. We would mark the first house with a number, and then our guide would say, for example, Yes, this house belongs to such and such person. We would frame the number assigned to that person. And then we would photograph the house in such a way as to ensure that the number assigned to that house was always shown in the photograph. In addition to that, Mr. Zvonko Djurdumovic also made sketches of houses we photographed. I hope this was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for that very detailed response. Now, this project began, or at least you physically went to Bosnia, in July of 1994, I believe the 7th.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. This project, if we can call it that way, was conducted in two stages, each stage lasting about ten days. The first one began on the 7th of August, and lasted for ten days or so. I remember that it lasted around ten days, because the work was very hard. We worked almost 16 hours a day. We would start at 7 a.m. and then work as long as it was daytime. And we had to travel between those locations, which would also consume some time. Therefore, as I told you, we worked in two stages, from the 7th until the 16th of July, and the second time was the second part of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that August 28th to the 31st of 1994? That was the second part of the project. And I referred to it as a project for lack of a better term, but to conduct the work that you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back briefly to the committee itself, do you know if there were any other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, once it has been raised by Judge Eser, I had noticed that also before, but in line -- page 22, line 3, the witness is reported as having the 7th of August, when in actual fact he did say 7th of July. He did -- if you look at lines 7 and 8 on the same page, you have a confirmation of that. But just for the record, 7th of August is being corrected to 7th of July. Yes, sorry, Ms. Richardson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the work of the committee, are you aware of any other individuals who were working with the commission with respect to documenting the damage to the villages that had occurred in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Based on our professional experience, and in view of that, we gave certain advice, professional advice. We told them that what we wanted us to do would be pointless if those who wanted to learn how these buildings had been damaged did not participate in that work. Our aim was also to establish who were the perpetrators of these acts. Therefore, we made a suggestion that, as members of the team, we should also have members or parties who had prior knowledge, who had local information, who had additional knowledge, and then we would participate in that team. And we also suggested that we should have some representatives of local authorities who would provide local information, such as who were the owners of the house, who were the victims, and so on. I don't know to this day whether they followed our recommendations, because we did our work on our own. When we completed the work that we were engaged to complete, I thought that it would be used for a number of purposes; to ensure that damages were paid, compensation was paid to the owners, because we knew that none of the houses were insured. So we hoped that this information would be used to ensure that the owners would receive compensation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the villages that were selected, were these primarily Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: One could say so. According to their information, the information provided by municipal authorities, yes. However, we didn't know that information. We simply used the information they had provided to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any international organisations involved in this -- with the committee and the work that you were conducting?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. This was one of several initiatives. In Belgrade, in the committee, there was always an initiative to involve international organisations in this work. However, we were unable to reach final agreement on the issue. And the similar situation existed in the territory where we worked. Despite the fact that the international community had their presence there, and the fact that we attempted to contact them, we were unable to involve them, and we relied on local Serb authorities only, as well as local guides who provided information to us as to what houses ought to be photographed and who were the owners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you arrived at a specific location, you said you believe that Jezestica was the first -- Bratunac municipality, Jezestica was the first village. Did you speak to the local people there to determine what had happened to that village. In other words, with respect to damage to the homes?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: No. I have to tell you that at the time when we visited these houses, a lot of people, almost majority of the residents, were gone. They were not there in the vicinity of their houses -- in their houses, because the houses could not be inhabited. They were in such a poor condition. However, it wasn't our job, it wasn't our task then to establish that. That was something that we had recommended should be done by somebody else, not by us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in 1992, some of these villages had been attacked, or there was an exchange, or that there was some type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't even need to hear the objection. Objection sustained, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in 1992 and 1993 -- I'll rephrase the question yet again. What -- prior to getting -- prior to going to the villages, were you told how the damage to the houses occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really object to this line of questioning for the following reason: This witness has been very clear that absolutely no part of his job involved trying to work out when damage was caused or by whom. If my learned friend, as she evidently is, is going to seek by all means to elicit some sort of hearsay evidence about what might have happened in 1992 and 1993, then it's completely inappropriate, firstly considering what type of witness we have here, but particularly in light of the very clear and honest answer he's given, which is that: That was never any part of my job, it was not a concern of mine. And a third point is a matter of disclosure. We have the statement of this witness, we have proofing notes. We've never seen anything which indicates these ever received any information about when any of the damage was caused. And so if that evidence is going to be given, who knows, we might have to adjourn to consider that evidence which we've never had sight of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't trying to elicit information from this witness about who caused the damage. I was simply trying to establish that, when -- without giving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't testify, because I can feel --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- don't testify instead of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is only a very simple question that he should be asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to ask the witness if he was aware that there was military activity in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't even -- I don't think -- I don't think you should put that question. It's the -- the question that should be put is very simply the following: Before you started your photographing tasks in relation to each particular municipality or village, were you given information by the authorities there, or by anyone, as to what you were going to photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And what were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They told us that we would be photographing houses, socially-owned property, churches, and individual monuments, perhaps even graveyards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were you told how come that all these houses, socially-owned houses, property, churches, individual monuments, et cetera, had come to be damaged? Were you given an indication at all? Or did you act on your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to remain within the sphere of hearsay, if that is any evidence for you, I can only tell you this: If it is true what they told us at the time, that many houses had been torched and some destroyed, that some monuments had been damaged by various weapons, they said that this is something that should be recorded. That's what they told us at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, to put it simply, you were quite aware that you were not going to photograph an earthquake zone, for example, where there had been devastation, you were going to photograph something completely different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I have not understood your question properly, but I'll say this again: They told us that we would be photographing houses that had burned down, houses that had been damaged, houses that had been partially torn down by the use of explosives, damage done to monuments and churches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to the work that you conducted, and how you went about conducting the work. You said that you had some -- that you were given, as a guide, a local person who would take you to the various houses, and would identify the owner of that house to you.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you were able to take photographs of all of the damaged houses in the village that you observed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Throughout our work, we were not photographing every single house, the reason being that our local guides, although we may have seen a of all of the damaged houses in the village that you observed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Throughout our work, we were not photographing every single house, the reason being that our local guides -- although we may have seen a person or two, of course. As I said, the reason being that our local guide could not point to every individual house and name the owner. They had no opportunity to consult with anyone on the ownership of a certain house. We wrote in our report that the sum total of our efforts, we tried to deal with this analytically, although what we conducted was not an analysis of whatever happened in the area. This was field work. It had to be quick; therefore, we did not go into any of this. But we didn't photograph every single house, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't photograph every single house that was damaged.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there other houses that you were unable to photograph because you were unable to -- because of its location, unable to get to them because of mines?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. If you go through our records you will notice that there are certain of houses that we were not able to reach because we were advised against that by our local guides. They did know a thing or two about an area being mined, which I had a chance to see for myself. On one occasion I had to remove it myself, but fortunately I escaped. If you look at these records, people identified certain houses. He said the second on the right belongs to such and such a person, and that other one over there belongs to that other person. We made a collective photograph in our records, and in that photograph you can see the names of owners the names of owners that we wrote down. But the image of the damage itself, the damage that occurred, is not really that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. My apologies to you, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you will need to repeat a little bit. I will help you, to tell you exactly from where you need to repeat because what you said has failed to go into the transcript. So we will have to go back a little bit, but I will tell you myself. Now, Mr. Jankovic, again, my apologies to you. We had a problem. You were asked a question, which I'm going to read out to you, and then you started giving an answer. But we stopped there because we had a technical hitch. The question that was put to you was the following: "And were there other houses that you were unable to photograph because you were unable to -- because of its location, unable to get to them because of mines?" And then you started answering, you said: "Yes. If you go through our records ..." And I remember what you said, but I think I cannot testify instead of you, so if you would kindly repeat your answer to Ms. Richardson's question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: I thank you, and I will now repeat what I said. If you go through our records, the documents that we have submitted to you, you will see that, in certain photographs, I'm not sure how many there are altogether, groups of houses were photographed, groups of three, four, or five houses. And then below the photograph, you have the names of owners. Our guides told us then, You see, the last house on the right belongs to such and such a person, and that one over there, to another person. The images are not clear as far as damage is concerned, because the photos were taken from a distance. But, for example, you can tell that certain houses did not have a roof. We didn't go there because we were advised against going by our guides. They said they were unsure themselves about certain areas that were or were not mined, that they used only those paths and only those roads that they knew for sure were safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you follow the same procedure, and that is, of having a local person identify the house -- the owner of the house to you, and then photographing the house? Did you place a number next to the house so that later on you were able to -- this would be part of your documentation system? And also later linked to the maps that were created.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And underneath the photographs, did you indicate the owner of the house, and did you also put additional information in some of the photographs as to how the damage occurred or what you observed? Not how the damage occurred, but whether it was damaged.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: If you have gone through our files carefully, you may have noticed differences in the captions below the photographs. Underneath some of the buildings, it said "Destroyed," underneath others, "Partially destroyed," and underneath yet others, "Rebuilt." This is the difference in our terminology. We deemed it necessary to define what we witnessed in these very terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses and the buildings that you photographed, were you able to tell what type of materials these buildings were made of? Was it -- in other words, was it brick or wood?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Once we completed the work that we were doing initially, no. But after we had seen a number of different buildings, we reached the conclusion that there were, in our assessment, three different types of buildings in the area. The first type would be buildings built on stone, on a stone surface, partially adobe and mud. Part of the building would be made in brick with a special structure between the two floors. And some of the buildings were relatively new, reinforced concrete and brick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go inside any of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what you observed from the inside of some of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We need to know which ones, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But also, what are you referring to? Because it's so generic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll get back to that question at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the photographs developed at some point? And could you tell us how long after you took the photos were they developed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: All the photographs we took from the very beginning, the first job we did between day one and day ten, the film rolls were developed after ten days of work. This was due to the fact that we did not have the technology needed in the area in which we worked. However, once this had been done, it constituted a very good basis for our further work. Therefore, at a later stage, it was no problem for us to piece the whole thing together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the photographing process, could you tell us, just generally, how you went about taking the photograph? Did you take -- what was your aim? And was it necessary at any point to examine the inside of any of the structures that you photographed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Our aim was - excuse me - to photograph as many buildings as possible as part of this project, but the aim was to photograph them in such a way as to get a general view, to try to take in the whole building. We would have loved, of course, had we only been able to, to take photographs from all the different angles so that one could get an idea of the entire building, as well as to take photographs of the interior. At the time, however, in view of the scope of the whole task in this specific area, as well as in many other areas in which we worked, it would have taken an enormous amount of time. Therefore, we decided to stick to the most basic kind of photograph, which is the general view, and what we have is what you can see in photographs of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because sometime, a few minutes ago or a few seconds ago, you did agree with Ms. Richardson that there were some instances in which you did enter into the house and took photos inside the house. What made you choose these houses in which you entered to take photos from the inside and not others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must enter a correction here, I'm afraid. I did go into houses but I did not take any photographs. Now, this is the one correction that I'm afraid I'll have to make. Now, why did we enter certain houses and not others? We entered those houses where it constituted no problem at all. We were able to do it in passing, to just enter and get a general impression on the state of the building. We did not have any reasons that were particularly important for us that led us to actually enter these houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, part of your assignment did not include you entering the houses to try and establish what could have caused the fire or the damage; that was not part of the assignment. Your assignment was basically to record, for posterity and for history, the condition of the house, or the houses, or the property, as it appeared to you at the moment you were taking the photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that we were recording this for posterity. That is one of the elements of our work. However, the fundamental objective was the following: Someone files a claim for damages for compensation. Our records would then form part and parcel of their claim. That is why we could not go into these buildings, or even try to define the total extent of damage. And this is something that we, at the time, advised the local authorities on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson, you've got two minutes before we break. Choose the appropriate time for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask one question before the break ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, at some point did you prepare a report memorialising your work and what you had -- the work you had conducted on behalf of the commission?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. Once our job was done -- we had taken notes, of course. And then once all of our work was done in the area, we drew up a report, including whatever we could, the nature of our work in the area, the specific buildings that had sustained damage, and so on and so forth. I think the report was written in late September or October. It is dated September, but the data were being gathered over quite an extended period of time. And it finally came out in October, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I think it would be appropriate to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Ms. Richardson. We'll have a break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, before the break, we were discussing -- you were testifying about your report, and that you had documented your findings and what you had photographed of the various villages, as requested by the committee. Now, as part of that report, did you prepare a table as well, showing the villages, the houses, as well as the person who identified the house to you, and that this table comprised your report as well?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, we compiled a table. The table was separate; however, it was attached to the report as a part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, I'd ask the usher's assistance in handing the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just confirm that the first page is, indeed, your report, which summarises what -- the work that you did in Eastern Bosnia on behalf of the committee.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second page indicates the damage to the various facilities in different villages.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And towards the end, there is a table overview of the documented facilities burned and destroyed during 1992 to 1993, at least that's what it says as part of that page, at the top of the page. It also lists, in the first column, the album number which corresponds to the village and the photographs. Would that be correct? I'm not sure you're looking at the right page.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at page 3, marked 01088658, and on that page, you see marked houses which were not privately owned. And these buildings are marked by their names. These are schools, monuments, and so on, socially-owned facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could give your attention to the usher for a moment, I'd have her place on the ELMO document with ERN 03599095, that is the B/C/S version. And if you could just take a look at that particular page and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please, if you could put it on the ELMO for the witness. Okay. Just a moment, Your Honour. If I could just hand the usher my copy for the record. Again, for the record, it's ERN 03 -- I apologise. I'll repeat. That's the B/C/S version of the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Jankovic, if you could just give your attention to the ELMO. All right. And is that the table that you referred to that illustrates the album number, the various villages, the buildings, and apartments, school, if there was one, industry and health care, if there was one, church and property and monuments, the photo numbers of the facility, as well as the information on who provided the owner of the particular structure that you photographed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In this table that we can see here, there are figures pertaining to the number of houses, number of socially-owned buildings, and also the photograph numbers, which is in the penultimate column. In the last column are the guides, the names of the guides who told us who the owners of certain houses were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this table also was part of your report.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for instance, in Jezestica, it indicates that there were 42 -- the number 42. And that number, if you could confirm, represents the number of houses that you photographed.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, the number of houses, so that means that there were 42 houses in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. There were 42 houses that you photographed, but there were not 42 houses in the village of Jezestica, were there? Or does this number only represent the buildings you photographed?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the -- this number 42 does not represent all of the houses that were damaged in Jezestica but only the ones you photographed. And you said before, those were the ones that a local person provided information on the ownership.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Ostojic Dusan, in Jezestica, was our guide who told us about the owners of 42 houses documented here. As for the others, I don't know. I don't know how many additional houses, in addition to the 42, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the same is true with respect to all of the villages that you were able to photograph, their structures, in that, for instance, number 2, in album number 2, Kravica, you list 48 houses. Now, that doesn't represent the total number of houses in Kravica but only the photographs that you took.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that these are not all of the houses. And the same goes for all other hamlets that I see in front of me right now. In some places, the number included every house, but in some places it did not. And I don't have any more detailed knowledge of it right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Next, I would -- that's all with respect to this particular document for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I thank the usher for her assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because we need to log this, this it a number. You're tendering it, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am tendering this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it is indispensable as part of your evidence. So this will be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 487, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 487. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, as part of your report, and as part of the work that you conducted, maps were prepared by yourself and Mr. Djurdumovic; is that correct? And with respect to the report that was just shown to you, Prosecution's Exhibit P487, you both authored this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one point with respect to your report, something that I'd like to point out. This report and the facilities that you photographed only represented about 75 per cent of the facilities in the area, of the various villages that you conducted your work in.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes. In that report, we wrote down that it was 75 per cent. It seemed like a good estimate at the time when we composed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, I'd like to turn your attention to the maps that were prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I'd ask the usher's assistance in handing this document - it's a map - to the witness. The document itself is a map. There are two pages. One is the map. The second page has signatures on it. So I'd like the witness to be shown the map. The additional page that's provided is the translation of the map, just for ease of -- just for Your Honours' benefit and everyone else's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look at this map, Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it also placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place it on the ELMO, with the usher's assistance. Mr. Jankovic, is this the map that you prepared? And tell us what this map -- what it represented in this map. And you can start with reading the top portion of the map so that we'll have it for the record.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In the upper portion of the map, it says "Committee for Gathering Data on Crimes Against Humanity and International Law, the Map of Central Drina River Area, East Bosnia." And then it says "Information on Houses Burnt Down and Destroyed," and then it gives the dates. This map was compiled by Zvonko Djurdumovic, and I assisted him, to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, and there is also a scale on this map, as well?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You can see the scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the lower left-hand map of the key has a key. And if you could just read out what that key states, the symbols as well as the explanation.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: I can't see them very clearly. There is a symbol for municipal centre. When the title was given to the map, it was given in general terms, and the term used was "Kravica"; however, the area covered is much wider. And then it says "Destroyed and Burned Places, Buildings, Facilities," and so on, and the photo number within the documentation. So here in this key, you can see what is shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps it would be easier for you to look at the document itself on the ELMO and not look at the screen. And if you could point to the key, is that easier for you to read. On the ELMO itself, look at the hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, I've already read it, as the usher was able to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's do this: This dot with the circle, does it represent the municipal centres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we don't need him to repeat that. He's explained it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. That's fine, Your Honour. I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated that -- if we could -- if you could -- if we could have a zoom-in on the Bratunac area on the map. Just by way of example, you said there are numbers there, and those numbers represent the houses from the various villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, I will explain that. Each circle on the map represents a house, and each number depicted here stands for just one house. In certain cases, which we explained previously, if several houses are marked with one number, then this is indicated. Since the map corresponds to the photo documentation, it is very easy to establish which number represents what house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was basically the same procedure for all of the villages and the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Identical, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. At this time I would tender this document, and if we could have a number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and received in evidence and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P488.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hear no objections from the Defence bench. I take it that there are none for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we have a point about the title, but it's a matter I'll raise in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And if I could have the usher's assistance with one more document, if this could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, could you take a look at this document. For the record 0108733, that's the ERN number. Now, this is another map, and was this also prepared for -- in connection with the work that you were conducting? And could you tell us if this is similar to the first map we just -- you just testified about?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This map that we're looking at now is practically a part of the previous map that we have just seen, and it is an integral part of the documentation but only for this limited area marked in red. All photo documentation has individual maps as integral parts of it with photographs taken and processed in that hamlet or in that place. However, all of that together is a part of the comprehensive map, and all of these maps were done in the same scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because, Ms. Richardson, this calls for an explanation. I notice, looking at the legend, that the damaged or destroyed property is the one coloured in red. And in fact, I remember, I recall, looking at the -- not the last document but the previous one, that in Jezestica, for example, you had indicated that there were 42 private homes that had been destroyed and one public building that had suffered damage. So here you are -- you find 43 buildings that are marked in red because they had sustained some damage. But I also see that in this map, there are many other dotted places, and the number reaches up to 167. The other buildings that are not -- that are not in red, do we take it that these buildings you did not -- you simply did not photograph, or do we also take it that these buildings were not damaged? What is the position? What are we supposed to understand when we look at this map and we see 43 buildings coloured in red and 124 buildings shown on the map but not coloured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's of any assistance, if it's any assistance, what do the numbers marked in red mean? The numbers marked in red refer to one photo file. The remaining numbers that you can see in this section of the plan, of the map, will reappear marked in red in the following photo file. And every single location on this map will have its own documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely what I had imagined it would be, but it --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to get to that point. Thank you for covering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have preempted your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I do appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think it was important, because you only have this one, and I know that there are others, because we have seen others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate it, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be marked P489. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, you -- the photographs that you took in Bosnia, in 1994, you had an opportunity to view these photographs after they were developed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you viewed these photographs in the Office of the Prosecution, and they were also shown to you by an investigator.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were the photographs that you took of the various villages as part of the work that you performed for the committee.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those photographs -- the structures in those photographs appeared to you as they did when you photographed them in 1994.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I would like the usher's assistance. We will hand out a sample of those photographs that were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, if we could have the photographs placed on the ELMO, one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I'd ask you to take a look at that photograph, ERN 010870 -- I'm sorry, 010878038. Also shown in that photograph is 01087839. The first photograph that you're viewing, is this a photograph that you took?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
