utterances.text: Yes, I took this. It's part of the files. On the face of it, I can't really say which group or which area this belongs to, since it's not part of the group as we see it here. But yes, essentially these are the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in this first photograph, if you could, in your opinion, tell us what you recognise as damage to this structure.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: By a purely visual inspection, I can see damage above one of the windows. There's a blackening. You can see this black patch, a darkening of the wall. I must say, though, that these photographs are copies. The ideal thing would be to look at the originals, obviously. But you can see this darkening here, this blot. Looking at this copy, it may be rather difficult for you to distinguish, but I do have an idea about what it might be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us what it might be? And could you point to the area that you're referring to on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This is a general impression and not a very specific impression. As you can see, this house has no windows or doors, so this may be a result of a fire inside the building, this building or a privately-owned house, as I prefer to define it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: The same applies to this other section. It is my assumption, but I am, in fact, positive about it, the entrance to the lower level of this house is, again, reflected in a darkening. Again, I must point out that this is a copy. The section just above the door, or below the first floor landing, the steps -- the stairs leading to the first floor of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, would you say that this fire was started from inside the house? And could you say if it was started by a grenade or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can he --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is where we will stop you. It's even unfair to ask the witness this question two years, almost two years after the event. And, I mean, it's not that big a deal if you ask him whether he thinks that the fire started from inside. I mean, there are no signs in the photo that there was a fire outside in any case. But to ask him whether that fire was precisely and particularly and specifically caused by a grenade, I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can take your point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure that he himself will not answer that question, or will try to avoid answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take your point with respect to grenade -- the grenade. But -- however, I think the witness can answer if -- based on his experience, whether, two years later, he can say anything with respect to the damage of the house. And I think that's a fairly -- that's a fair question, his experience of two years later --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I put some questions earlier on, because precisely the witness has already stated or told us what his task was. His task was to record the -- at face value, the damage that he could visualise, moving from one house or from one building to the other, so that then, those photos could serve a purpose later on, be it for historical, be it for possible claims of damages, be it for possible compensation, and so on and so forth. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, mostly I'd respectfully adopt everything Your Honour has just said. Two points, really. My learned friend doesn't seem to have taken on board the fact that if we're asking this witness to give an opinion based on experience, that's expertise, that's one of the characteristics of an expert. Based on his experience, he gives an opinion which the layman might not be able to provide. And he's not an expert. If he were an expert, we would have 94 bis and also some other problems. As far as anything which can conclude on the basis of the photograph is concerned, we can draw the same conclusions. And that's why the exercise is futile. Because if all he's to say is, Well there's a blackening above the door or window, well, we can see that. And the exercise will become very protracted because I will have to go through all these photographs myself and make observations about holes in roofs and things like that, which also have --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only exercise that would make sense, but, again, I'm -- I'm prepared to discuss this with everyone here --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and go through the whole exercise if necessary. But if a witness comes forward and says, Well, I saw this house being set on fire on such and such a date by means of hand grenades that were thrown into the building, and then you ask the witness whether that would be compatible with what he visualised two years later, I mean that is okay. But, again, we have got the passage of time, two years later, and in the absence of that much evidence put in place, I mean, you're still operating in a huge vacuum here, because in two years' time -- in two years anything could have happened. In two years, it could have been set on fire again, it could have been further destroyed, it could have been -- anything could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I will leave it -- I would just like to hear what the witness has to say about this, because he is a professional man. I mean, the moment he started giving evidence, you can see that he is a highly trained and a very professional -- a very professional man. I mean, are you prepared to, while you're sitting there and answering questions, tell us how this fire came to be, what caused the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first reason that, professionally speaking, I would not put myself in that position is precisely what you have just spoken about. A lot of time has gone by since. Of course, it may have occurred at any given point in time throughout that period. It is certainly not my place to specify the day. From a professional point of view, it would be very difficult for me. If Your Honours insist on my opinion, I could, perhaps, provide it, but it would be extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There you are, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just respond briefly. I am aware, and the point is taken, that it was two years after the fact, and anything could have happened during that period of time. However, we have heard testimonies -- testimony from various witnesses who either observed their houses being set on fire, or who -- going through the village. So that is the link, Your Honour. This witness is simply here who sought -- person saw the structure, who took the photograph, who documented the damage to the structure. And I take issue with counsel who states that, asking the witness, in his experience. We've had witnesses here who've been repeatedly asked about their experience and what caused the damage, and it was not a problem then. I only asked this of this witness because he does have experience in investigating crime scenes, and if he could tell us, two years later, what he was able to determine, looking at the structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two years, this is precisely why I won't allow you to ask the question. Because I know that asking the witness to explain, on the basis of a photograph, or on the basis of what he could see visually on the spot, what had caused a fire -- the fire two years earlier, you're even being specific. You're telling him when the fire -- I mean, how can he know when the place was set on fire or when the explosion took place? He doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- he wasn't there when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have got the other witnesses. Stick to those. And with this witness, you just ask him to confirm that this is a photo he took, and that it showed at the time soot or blackening which is indicative that there was a fire at some point in time inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will withdraw my question with respect to the grenade and what caused the fire. Your point is noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to show the witness the next -- the photo of the houses on the next page, which is 01087840.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, ask Mr. Jankovic if you recognise this photograph, one of the photographs that you took as part of the project. And could you tell us what damage you see to the house from the photograph, and what you recall.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Yes, these are the photographs I took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see any damage to the house which would indicate that there was a fire?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: The same applies as to the previous photograph. The damage to this house can be clearly seen. It should be easy enough for a layman, and even easier for a person like me. Now, when did this damage come about, and what caused it? This is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clearly, and that's not my question. I'm simply asking if you're able to recognise from this photograph that there was a fire. And could you tell us if this fire was started from the inside, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: The same applies as to the previous series of photographs. There is no substantial damage on the outside. These blackenings, the dark spots or patches that you can see, are clearly a result of something that occurred inside the house. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think, Ms. Richardson, the witness is teaching us all a lesson. How can you expect Mr. Jankovic to tell us, answering your question, whether the fire was started from inside? It will take an expert to come to that conclusion. And the witness has told us that there were very few houses in which he actually went in, and he didn't go into those houses to establish whether the fire or the damage had started from inside. How can he do it two years after the fact? It could have started outside, moved into inside, and what we see here is the result of the fire that was happening at some point in time on the inside. But it's not necessarily that it was started inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps we can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a short break of about five minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's proceed. Mr. Jankovic, while we are going through some of these photographs, I suppose -- don't think we're going through the entire --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's just a sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there are any remarks or comments that you would like to make with regard to any particular photo that you are being asked questions about, please go ahead. I mean, don't wait for questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example, let me give you an idea. If, say, looking at, I don't know, the photo -- the fourth photo on the second page, the one in the bottom, you see blackening outside the left-hand window or veranda door and you think that that blackening is not the result of fire -- no, the bottom one, the second page. It's S1-5, number 5, photograph number 5. If you, for example -- that blackening above the left-hand door or window at first-floor level, according to you, is not the result of fire but is the result of, for example, mold or something else that could have blackened the appearance of the building, then, of course, please do point out that to us. In other words, if there is something that we may mistake for signs of fire which are not signs of fire but the signs of something else, then do let us know, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us focus on the photographs, or rather, by photographs alone, it would be difficult to establish what caused the damage. However, I was present there, I saw all of this with my own eyes. I took pictures of it, and now I comment on these pictures. So now I am giving you my impression from that time. So if we take this approach, then this photograph marked 5, and the one marked 4, I can say a very similar thing: Some have black marks, some have floors that have completely burnt down, but since these are brick structures, I can say that if we were to disregard shadows that can be seen in certain photographs, depending on what time of the day the picture was taken - sometimes we took pictures in the morning, sometimes in the evening - so if we were to disregard the shadows, then we would still be able to see some details that I can give you my opinion of. I hope this is clear. These are the black marks that can come about as a result of a fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are black marks on any photo that you think may not or could not be the result of fire, then please do indicate those to us so that we will be aware of them. Because we are not experts like you are, and as you said, after all, you are the one who took these photos, and you were on site when you took them. Yes, Ms. Richardson. I'm making your life difficult this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour. I appreciate your assistance. If I could have the usher turn to the next two photographs, 10 and 11, and that is ERN number 01087846 and 01087847. Now, again, these are not the originals, and they are photocopied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd appreciate, Mr. Jankovic, your impressions, as you're looking through the photographs, as well as going back to your memory, as to what you observed on these two structures.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: I want to be sure that you understand my evidence properly. The photograph marked with number 10, we keep referring to these black marks which are a result of the movement of the smoke, not necessarily the fire itself, just the way that smoke moved. But we already said that we are not going to comment on the causes of fire. But here, above this small window, and here, by the entrance, which is an entrance into the house, you can see black marks. As I've said, this is something that you will see in numerous pictures which are part of this photo file. The same can be said of the photograph marked with number 11. However, even on this picture -- looking at this picture, it is difficult to give a comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to photograph number 10, it appears, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, this -- could you tell us about this particular structure. It appears as though the roof on this structure is undamaged, and could you tell us a little bit about that, and whether you recall the condition of this roof when you took the picture.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: I cannot remember this house specifically. However, in certain houses, in certain cases, the owners, in order to preserve the house, to prevent any further deterioration, rebuilt just the roofs on their houses and prevented further damage. This is one of such cases. In some other pictures, if you zoom in, you will be able to see that the roofs are newly built.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next set of photographs, 16, 17, ERN number 01087852 and 853. Looking at these two photographs, could you tell us what are your impressions with respect to these photographs, and anything that you observed on that day, whether there was any damage caused by fire or anything else. And also, if you could tell us what types of structures these two -- these two buildings are made of. Is it brick, wood, or anything -- other type of material?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This house belongs to the second group. As I've told you initially, there were three groups of buildings, and this house would belong to the second group. It was built of brick, and the construction in between the floors was built out of wood, so in a somewhat different way than the houses built of reinforced concrete. Normally, in such cases, only the walls remained. Everything else that was constructed simply deteriorated and was destroyed and collapsed in a pile inside the house. So if you stood next to the house, even without entering the house, you would be able to see this construction material, wood piled in the middle of the house. I couldn't tell you how many such houses there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said this wood that would be in the middle of the house as a result, could you -- do you recall if there was any indications of a fire?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In cases such as this, where lime was used, the water washed it out to such an extent that it was impossible to say even then, let alone now based on the photographs, what exactly had caused it. There was so much water damage, and so much was washed out by water, that even plants started growing inside the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn to the next two photographs, and if there's anything specific that you'd like to indicate regarding these two structures. In fact, I think the second one, ERN 01087861, I think, we can leave out. Just the first structure, which is 01087860. If you could comment on that structure, and if you recall if there were any indications of fire that you remember.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: As you can see, the owners of these houses who came to visit their homes cleaned the area so that the construction material which had caved in was now taken to the middle of the house. This house belongs to the same category as the previous one, and it is very difficult now to say what exactly had caused the house to look as it looks nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn to the next photograph, and specifically the photograph at the bottom of the page, ERN 01087867. Now, you took this photograph of this structure. Could you tell us why this photograph was taken, and whether you had any impressions at the time.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: If you are referring to photograph 131 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This house and similar, unfinished houses were photographed because, in certain cases, it was obvious that the construction material had been hauled away; windows, doors, even roof construction. I couldn't tell you now who had taken it. However, this is what the guides told us. Therefore, houses such as this one were photographed, although there were not that many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of those houses where you said the materials had been taken away, was there any indication that you recall, I know -- I don't think we have a photograph of that example that you're giving, but was any indication of fire of those structures, even though it was apparent that people had taken some of the material away? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: No. In this particular case, in this photograph, there was no fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next couple of photographs, 01087870 and 871, specifically focusing on 870. Could you tell us what your impressions are, at that time and now, of the damage to this particular house.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: Now, just as then, we can see that this house had been fired upon. I don't know what certain units at the time used as weapons. However, what we can see now is that part of the roof has caved in. There's damage to the windows and walls. But I couldn't tell you more about the specific weapon used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the next set of photographs, 010 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next set of photographs we'll look at, 01087874 and 875. Could you tell us what your impressions were of these two structures, and if there were any indications of a fire or anything else.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: As in previous cases, we can see -- or rather, as in the previous case, we can see here, in these two photographs -- I can tell you that my assumption is that the damage here is identical to the one we saw in photograph 131, naturally, without the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the next two photographs, 01087995, just focusing on that particular area. Now, there's no house there. Could you tell us what your impressions were at that time of whatever is left of, I assume, a house, at one point.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This house, marked 140, belongs to the third group of houses, in the construction of which, mud, hay, and solid construction material was used. The foundation was made out of stone, and everything that was used between the storeys was termed light construction material. In this case, this is all that remained, just a pile of dirt covered by weeds. The house marked 141 is a house that was also fired upon. I couldn't be more specific as to the weapon from which they fired. The damage is great. There was no fire here, but you can see what damage was caused to this house built of reinforced concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not go through all of the photographs. I'll just select the remaining few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look at number 176, ERN 01088038, and tell us what your impressions are with respect to the structure we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because you said, according, at least, to the transcript that I have here, is photograph 176, ERN 038. What we have on the screen is 176. All right, but that is not 037 -- not 038 but 037.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't know which one you want to show --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's 037, Your Honour, the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir if you could just look at this structure and tell us what your impressions were of the damage to this structure.

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: This photograph is marked 176. This is an old building with brick used here, no reinforced concrete. Looking at this photograph, and bearing in mind at the same time what I saw on the spot, on some of the buildings, you can see small spots which is the form of damage to the wall of this house. If you expect me to base my judgement on this photograph only, it could be interpreted in any number of ways. However, since I personally looked at these buildings on the ground, I could tell that these are pockmarks, because the walls were hit by missiles. My conclusion at the time was that there had been fighting going on in the area and around these houses, but nothing more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at this last photograph that I'll be showing you for now, that is, ERN 01088470, it's marked as photograph number 603. Do you recall this particular -- I believe it was at one point a house. Do you recall taking this photograph and visiting this particular structure?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. My memory can hardly be expected to be that good, in view of the total number of buildings under consideration. But this other one, I think this is the building that we spoke about a moment ago, a mud and straw building. It is quite ruined. This section you can see over here, what remains of the house was used as some sort of a larder, a pantry, or even as a barn, to keep cattle. And then above was this house made of mud, straw, and wooden beams, that I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- do you recall seeing any evidence of a fire with respect to this structure when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
utterances.text: In buildings of this type, that is something that is impossible to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher, for your assistance. Your Honour, at this time, and Mr. Jankovic, at this time, the Prosecution would seek to tender the photographs taken by Mr. Jankovic, and that is ERN 0107832, 01087879 to 0108847-- 447, 0108-8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go slower, please, because I don't want mistakes to be made, or to appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Specifically, Your Honour, just for clarification, I'll repeat the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the photographs that we are now tendering were the photographs taken by Mr. Jankovic with all of the markings as were originally made to the photographs. They are very different from the ones that were used by the witnesses where we took out the information that was put in by Mr. Jankovic. So at this point, we're seeking to tender that whole range of photographs taken by Mr. Jankovic as part of the project, and that -- those photographs are contained, as well as the map of each village, and that is specifically ERN number ERN 010-7832 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I guess this is already in as P489.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is all going to be very much confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, you have used this bundle of photographs --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which is only an infinitesimal, small part of the whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is what you relied upon not even totally when examining this witness. Why don't you signal this set of photos separately as the photos out of which you used some when examining the witness, and present it, or file it, tender it, as just one new document, irrespective of the fact that some of these photos we have seen during other -- testimony of other persons, and some we'll probably see during the testimony of persons that have still got to come, I don't know. But you can select this as the specimen that you used for the purpose of this witness only, and tender it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a good idea. So at this point, I'd like to tender this group of photographs that were used during the testimony of Mr. Jankovic, and I believe the ERN number's already in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, there is an additional -- I just need a minute to discuss with my case manager, Your Honour, the tendering of other photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gerold, can you count the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. At this time --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, because I do not know whether Ms. Richardson agrees with this or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do agree with placing into evidence the photographs that were used by Mr. Jankovic -- with Mr. Jankovic during his testimony. What we also have, his entire file, of all of the photographs, and we will submit that as well, and I believe that can be 365 point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with this first. For the record, the Prosecution is tendering as Exhibit P489?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 490, 38 photographs contained in 19 pages, with a non-sequential ERN numbering; this being the specimen that she used during the examination-in-chief of Witness Jankovic, Dragan. Jankovic Dragan. Yes, now you may proceed with the rest. And there is -- I suppose there shouldn't be any problems forthcoming from the Defence. The Prosecution is, from what I can see, offering to tender these photos in electronic format.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the other exhibits, previously tendered on January 10th, we have copies of the photographs, and these are without captions that were used with our witnesses. And this is Prosecution Exhibit 365.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you give it to me, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. The clarification -- I believe there's a clarification. This is an entire set of the photographs. Some were used -- some of the -- some of the photographs were used with our witnesses, but this is the entire set, without captions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this, I take it, is a replication of what we should already have in the record, because it shows P365 here. Has P365 been tendered already, or has it just been prenumbered but not tendered yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll need the represent of the case managers here and the registrar. Do you have P365 on record already? Yes, please go ahead. Your microphone, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was on the 15th of October, 2004. The Prosecutor submitted a set of photographs which was marked as P365, but it was marked only for identification on the very day. This set of photographs contained comments and therefore the Trial Chamber asked the Prosecutor to tender another clean set of documents and to substitute the provision. So on the 22nd of October, the Prosecutor tendered a clean version, and this clean version substituted, then, the old versions. The old versions were taken out of the record, and this new set got the number P365, marked for identification. Then in January, when Witness Manas was here, the Prosecutor sought to add to this P365 additional -- a lot of additional photos, the whole set, but they didn't have all the documents here. Therefore, we put on the record that these additional photographs should be all under P365, and the Prosecutor announced he would provide, in the near future, these additional pictures. Now, I was told informally by the Prosecutor that -- we agreed, actually, that it might be better to keep the old and initial pictures marked for identification as P365, and tender all the -- the whole set as P365.1. And this would be on the CD-ROMs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's very well put and also practical. Do the parties agree to that approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we're happy with that. We may have to check whether we've got ones with captions or without captions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These will be without captions, supposedly, according to what the Prosecution is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, well, then, we need to receive that then, because the current one we have has captions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the old one which supposedly we have already removed from the record, and which the registrar is suggesting that we should get back. And I agree because I don't think it should have been removed in the first place even for purposes of comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just that for this witness, I was going to show pictures from the CD, and it was evidently the old ones with captions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry. With this witness you can show from -- photos from the old --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem. So do you agree with this approach as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and thank you to the registrar for that very detailed clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My suggestion goes a little bit beyond what you have stated, Mr. Siller, Mr. Registrar, in that I would prefer to have all three versions put on record. The original, which was tendered for identification, will remain in the record as P365. The next set, which was submitted in replacement of the first one, without the name plates and without indications, will be 365.1. And this new set will be P365.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I take it from what Ms. Richardson said, that these do not contain comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Those have no captions. We do have an additional exhibit which contains the captions as well as the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that can now replace the original 365. That can replace the original 365, because it's more complete in the sense that it contains more photos than what you had originally tendered for identification purposes, I take it. I see the case manager nodding.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I just have one clarification that I need to seek, and that is, I know we introduced certain photographs with certain witnesses and those were without the captions. And so I just want to make sure that we keep that record straight with respect to the photographs that were used with certain witnesses, and now we have -- so I guess, in essence, what we will have is exhibits which are in full, a full copy with the captions, a foul copy without the captions, and then exhibits that were used with specific witnesses. I don't know if that, sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, then I will keep everything on record. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm making it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, we are not going -- but I don't agree with having a system whereby documents come in the record and then disappear and are substituted. They may be substituted, but they should also remain in the records. So what we will have is the original set tendered for identification which will remain marked as P365. We will have the first -- the set that was tendered subsequently, without the captions, which will be 365.1; right? Then we have this new set that you are tendering now with the captions but with additional photos, and that will be 366. Why not have it 366, as a new -- because the first two would have been the first two batches. Now these are absolutely new. This is the clean sheet that we have. So we'll give it a different number. The "replacement" of 365 would be 366, and the replacement of 365.1 will be 366.1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it can't be 366 because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already taken by something else.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- the numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So then that batch will be 365.2, and this, the one they gave us a few minutes ago, will be 365.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, that's fine with me, and I think my case manager --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today you are tendering two sets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One is a replication of the first set that you had tendered for identification but with the addition of new photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That is going to be 365.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? Already we have on the record 365 and 365.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are old sets that you tendered months ago, or weeks ago. Now we are going to have two sets today. That is one, the first one. That will be 365.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With comments, with captions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With captions. And the one without captions will be 365.3. And please do say that that contains six CDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we inadvertently gave you an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I see, I see. We'll take one each, and I give you four, and you give me one of the others -- three of the others. These need to be marked straightaway. This is three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, I thank you. I know that this was not easy, but at the same time we tried to take a practical -- as much of a practical approach as possible. It's never easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we will adjourn for today, because I have to start with an initial appearance very soon. Mr. Jankovic, we have to stop here today, and you will return tomorrow. And it should be over within a relatively short time. Then you can return back to your country. I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: witness:  If I ask you to walk into a building that has burnt down, say,
